title: Linux Boot Process Quick Revision
summary: A night-before revision of how Linux boots, from firmware and GRUB through kernel, initramfs and systemd, plus the everyday commands for inspecting boot, logs, modules and kernel version.

chapters.title: Boot Chain: The Mental Model
points: Boot order: firmware (BIOS/UEFI) → bootloader (GRUB) → kernel + initramfs → systemd (PID 1) → target reached
Each stage only loads the next one and hands over control; a failure points to the stage that never finished
BIOS reads the MBR (first 512 bytes of the disk) and runs the boot code in it; UEFI reads .efi files from the EFI System Partition (FAT32)
POST (power-on self-test) runs in firmware first, then firmware picks the boot device from its boot order
The kernel is the first thing that talks to hardware; systemd is the first userspace process (PID 1) and parent of all others

chapters.title: Firmware and GRUB
points: BIOS vs UEFI: BIOS uses MBR and legacy 16-bit code with disks up to 2 TB; UEFI uses GPT, the ESP and supports Secure Boot and disks above 2 TB
Check which mode is running: ls /sys/firmware/efi exists only when booted in UEFI mode
GRUB config is generated, not hand-edited: edit /etc/default/grub, then run update-grub (Debian/Ubuntu) or grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (RHEL)
Common /etc/default/grub keys: GRUB_TIMEOUT, GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT (e.g. quiet splash), GRUB_DEFAULT (which entry boots)
At the GRUB menu press e to edit an entry once (add single, init=/bin/bash or systemd.unit=rescue.target), then Ctrl+X to boot; changes are not saved

chapters.title: Kernel and initramfs
points: GRUB loads two files from /boot: vmlinuz-<version> (compressed kernel) and initramfs-<version>.img (initrd) and passes the kernel command line
initramfs is a temporary root filesystem in RAM holding the drivers (disk, LVM, RAID, LUKS) needed to find and mount the real root
After mounting the real root, the kernel switches to it and executes /sbin/init, which is a symlink to systemd
View the arguments the running kernel got: cat /proc/cmdline (e.g. root=UUID=... ro quiet)
Rebuild initramfs after changing drivers or disk setup: update-initramfs -u (Debian/Ubuntu) or dracut -f (RHEL); a missing driver gives 'cannot mount root' or a dracut emergency shell

chapters.title: systemd, Targets and Boot Logs
points: systemd is PID 1: it starts units (services, mounts, sockets) in parallel according to their dependencies, and reaps orphan processes
A target groups units into a boot goal: multi-user.target (text, no GUI), graphical.target (GUI), rescue.target (single user), emergency.target (minimal shell), poweroff.target
Default target: systemctl get-default and systemctl set-default multi-user.target; switch live with systemctl isolate rescue.target
Boot logs: dmesg shows the kernel ring buffer (hardware, drivers); journalctl -b shows the whole current boot, journalctl -b -1 the previous boot, journalctl -b -p err only errors
Slow boot analysis: systemd-analyze for total time, systemd-analyze blame for the slowest units, systemctl --failed for units that failed

chapters.title: Kernel Modules and uname
points: Kernel modules are .ko drivers loaded and unloaded at runtime without a reboot, stored under /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/
lsmod lists loaded modules with size and used-by count; modinfo <mod> shows description, parameters and dependencies
modprobe <mod> loads a module and its dependencies; modprobe -r <mod> unloads it; insmod/rmmod do the same without resolving dependencies, so prefer modprobe
Load at boot via /etc/modules-load.d/*.conf; block a driver with 'blacklist <mod>' in /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf; a module in use (non-zero used-by) cannot be removed

uname -r gives the kernel release, uname -a everything, uname -m the architecture; after a kernel update the running kernel stays old until reboot, which is why modprobe can fail with 'module not found' when /lib/modules/$(uname -r) is gone

chapters.title: Boot Cheat Sheet
points: Order: firmware → GRUB → kernel + initramfs → systemd → target
Firmware: ls /sys/firmware/efi (UEFI check); GRUB: edit /etc/default/grub then update-grub; cat /proc/cmdline
Targets: systemctl get-default | set-default <t> | isolate <t>; rescue: add systemd.unit=rescue.target at GRUB
Logs: dmesg, journalctl -b, journalctl -b -1, journalctl -b -p err, systemd-analyze blame, systemctl --failed
Modules and version: lsmod, modinfo, modprobe/modprobe -r, blacklist in /etc/modprobe.d/, uname -r/-a/-m; rebuild initramfs with update-initramfs -u or dracut -f
